Indians in Pakistani Jails 
*401. SHRI RAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR REDDY:† 
SHRI AMAR SINGH: 
Will the Minister of EXTERNAL AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) the number of Indian civil prisones and fishermen in Pakistani 
jails, at present; 
(b) the number of Pakistani prisoners and fishermen in Indian jails, at 
present; 
(c) the steps being taken to get them released from the respective 
countries; 
(d) whether Pakistan has given any assurance in this regard; and 
(e) if so the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS (SHRI DIGVIJAY SINGH): (a) to (e) A Statement is placed on 
the Table of the House. 
Statement 
As per available information following numbers of Indian and Pakistani 
civilian prisoners and fishermen are detained in each other's jails. 
Indian Prisoners Pakistani Prisoners 
in Pakistan in India

RAJYA SABHA [21 August, 2003] 
Government, after their jail sentence is over. Government have 
consistently taken up the matter of release of Indian civilian prisoners 
and fishermen detained in Pakistan. As a result, Pakistan provided consular 
access to 110 Indian civilian prisoners  during 2002-03. Out of these, 20 
prisoners were repatriated on 18.5.2003 . Nationality of another 80 prisoners 
has been confirmed to Government of Pakistan who have been requested 
to fix an early date for their release. Response from Pakistan is awaited. 
Nationality verification of remaining 10  civilan prisoners is under process. 
Government have also confirmed the nationality of 319 Indian fishermen 
detained in Pakistan. A 6 member fishermen association's delegation 
from Gujarat is currently in Pakistan for carrying out the repairs of boats 
to facilitate the early repatriation of detained fishermen. 
Government provided consular access to 87 Pakistani civilian 
prisoners and 93 fishermen during the year 2002-03. Of these, 6 Pakistani 
civilian prisoners, whose nationality was confirmed, were released on 
25.6.2003. A Pakistani fishermen association's delegation is scheduled 
to visit Indian shortly to carry out re pairs of boats to facilitate repatriation 
of detained Pakistani fishermen. 
SHRI RAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR REDDY: Sir, there are about 868 
civilians and 319 poor fishermen in the Pakistani jails. I would like to 
know from the hon. Minister the details of Pakistani prisoners in Indian 
jails for more than ten years, the directions of the Supreme Court given 
to the Indian Government in this regard, and also, the position with regard 
to Indian prisoners lodged in Pakistani jails. 
SHRI DIGVIJAY SINGH: Sir, as regards the question of Indian 
prisoners in Pakistani jails, they broadly fall under four categories: detained 
fishermen, civilian prisoners, prisoner s of war, and others. In the last 
category are persons whom Pakistan has wrongly accused of spying and 
such activities, and sometimes, classified them as security prisoners. 
The protocol on consular access signed between the two countries 
in 1982 covers the categories of pris oners who are not apprehended for 
political or security reasons or offe nces. There is a set procedure for 
release of detained fishermen and civ ilians. Release of those in the fourth 
category is normally sought through exchanges.

SHRI N. JOTHI: Sir, it is a routine affair for Rameshwaram fishermen 
to be taken away by the Sri Lankan Navy or by the Sri Lankan fishermen. 
It is happening daily. Daily twenty, thirty or fifty fishermen are taken 
away. Not even a single day goes without these people being caught by 
them. Whenever the question is raised, law and order problem arises in 
Tamil Nadu. Our Chief Minister has al so written letters to  various Offices 
or Ministries here. But it is going on like this. Neither the Coast Guard is 
taking any action in this regard nor the Ministry of External Affairs seems 
to be having any permanent solution of this issue. My question is: What 
are the concrete steps taken by the G overnment of India to prevent this 
kind of affairs? Will there be any agenda to take back Kachchathivu 
Island that has been wrongly given to Sri Lanka? It is very near 
Rameshwaram. They say that their coastal area territorial boundary 
extends up to that island. What is the permanent solution that the 
Government has got for this issue? It is a daily menace that is going on. 
Is the Ministry aware of this? We would like to know about this. 
THE MINISTER OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS (SHRI YASHWANT 
SINHA): Sir, on the question of Indian fishermen straying across the 
international boundary into Sri Lankan waters, as far as that issue is 
concerned, we are in touch with the very friendly Government of Sri 
Lanka, and from time to time we make sure that through intervention of 
our High Commission in Sri Lanka these fishermen are released. But it is 
a fact, Sir, that often despite the clear demarcation of the international 
waters of the two countries, fishermen stray across into the Sri Lankan 
waters. We have advised the Governme nt of Tamil Nadu; we have advised 
the fishermen's associations to be careful with regard to this so that 
these incidents do not arise, but even  after this, as I said, whenever 
such a situation arises, when our fishermen are apprehended by the Sri

Lankan authorities, then, we immediat ely intervene. I personally know of 
many cases where our intervention has been effective and the fishermen 
have been released. I was, Sir, s upposed to go to Sri Lanka on the 19th 
and 20th; I could not for other reasons. But, this was one of the issues 
that I had proposed to take up with them. Whenever we get an opportunity 
to apprise the Sri Lankan autorities of  our concerns, we do so; we will 
continue to do so; we are trying to workout institutional arrangement with 
the Sri Lankan authorities. I would like to assure this House that in this 
matter, we have received the fullest  co-operation of the Sri Lankan 
authorities, unlike in the case of Pakistan where such co-operation is not 
always forthcoming. In the case of Sri Lanka, such co-operation is always 
forthcoming. 
As far as Kachchathivu Island is concerned, it has been repeatedly 
stated, decided, confirmed even by the Government of India that this 
Island falls in Sri Lankan waters, that  we have no sovereign right over 
this. It is only a question of our fishermen getting some concession from 
the Sri Lankan Government so that they could, perhaps, dry their nets, 
etc. They can't fish in those waters around Kachchathivu Island, but some 
facilities, like drying of nets, etc., is something which is under negotiations.

Telecom Service Providers for non provision of committed number of

Licences granted for operation of Basic Service in 1997-1998 to six 
private companies stipulated that Village Public Telephones will be provided 
in 97806 villages as a part of Roll-Out obligations. All of them have not 
been able to fulfil their obligations in the stipulated time frame. The details 
are given in the Statement-1 (See below). 
Since the process of setting up of VPTs by the Private Basic Service 
Operators is still being pursued and has not yet been completed, the 
calculation of loss of Rs. 720 crore would not be correct. 
The steps being taken to provide rural phones during the year 2003- 
2004 are as follows :— 
(i)  Bharat Sanchar Nigam Limited (BSNL) has drawn up plans to 
provide 8.6 lakh connections in rural areas during 2003-2004. 
(ii)  Notices have been issued in May, 2003 to Private Basic Service  
Operators to provide VPTs as well as submit plans to provide 
balance VPTs by the end of 2003 after excluding the categories 
of villages identified as de-populated villages, villages with 
population less than 100, Naxalite or insurgency affected villages 
and to be covered by satellite media in the first phase, failing 
which steps for encashment of the Performance Bank Guarantee 
will be initiated. The fulfilment of the commitments given by the 
Private Basic Service Operators is closely monitored and 
Performance Bank Guarantee would be liable to be encashed in 
case of failure. 
(iii) BSNL has planned to provide 11063 VPTs using Wireless in 
Local Loop (WLL) technology during 2003-2004. The balance 
18006 VPTs will be set up via Satellite media subject to availability 
of funds. 
(iv) The Bill to establish Universal Service Obligatbn Fund has been 
introduced in the Lok Sabha. It is proposed to provide support to 
the various Service Providers for maintenance of VPTs and 
replacement of MARR based VPTs, from this Fund.

Cost escalation of infrastructure projects 
*418. SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: Will the PRIME MINISTER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether slippage in implementation of major infrastructure projects 
like roads, railways and power has resulted in cost escalation of projects; 
(b) if so, the percentage of escalation in cost as originally envisaged; 
(c) whether these projects have also been delayed; and 
(d) the steps taken or proposed to be taken to check the escalation 
of cost and expedite the completion of projects? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF STATISTICS AND 
PROGRAMME IMPLEMENTATION (SHRI SATYABRATA 
MOOKHERJEE): (a) to (d) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) Yes, Sir. The percentage of cost escalation with respect to 
the original approved cost in respect of major projects costing Rs. 100 
crore and above in roads, railways and power sectors are 3,54.5 and 35 
respectively. 
(c) and (d) Yes, Sir. The steps taken to check the escalation of cost 
and complete the projects within schedule are as follows: 
(i)   Adoption of two- stage clearance system a nd stricter appraisal 
of project reports before investment approval; 
(ii)   Taking up of projects for implementation only after funds have 
been fully tied up; 
(iii) In-depth review of projects on monthly as well as quarterly basis 
by the Government; 
(iv) Follow up with the State Governments in respect of problems 
relating to acquisition of land, re habilitation related issues, forest 
clearances, provision of infrastruc ture facilities and ensuring law 
and order at project sites, etc. 
(v) Setting up of ah Empowered Committee in the administrative 
Ministries for review of departmentally executed projects; 
27 

RAJYA SABHA [21 August, 2003] 
(vi)   Inter-ministerial coordination for resolving unresolved problems; 
(vii) Setting up of Standing Committees in the Ministries/Departments 
to fix responsibility for time and cost overruns; 
(viii) Appointment of nodal officers fo r each project with continuity of 
tenure; and 
(ix)   Issue of guidelines on standard bidding documents for adoption. 
SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: Sir, a very big problem which we 
face in our country is the delay in execution of projects which eventually 
leads to cost overrun of these pr ojects. The Government has accepted 
that as for roads, railways and powe r sectors, the percentages of cost 
escalation are 3,54.4 and 35 respectively. Sir, I want to draw the attention 
of the Government as to how private-public partnership, which is a new 
concept that has been envisaged by our Government, — this is being 
used as a strategy to set up infrastructural development by both the 
State Governments and the Central Government — is being exploited by 
the private sector, or to say, the private promoters, to substantially over- 
state the projects. Also, this has go t a tremendous adverse impact on 
the utility charges that are being levied by the Government. The best 
example is Enron. So, does the Government have any proposal to review, 
especially in power projects, the Po wer Purchase Agreements that have 
been entered into by them and by the other Governments, and correct 
such propaganda? 
SHRI SATYABRATA MOOKHERJEE: Sir,  this particular aspect of 
the matter really does not concern this question. It relates to the Central 
sector projects which are under implementation. And, as of 1st April, 
2003, there are 540 projects costing over Rs. 20 crores. But the real 
backlog is in respect of 30 projects which account for about 95 per cent 
of the cost overrun. I can just read them out; it is a very short table 
where the details of these projects have been given. So far as Power 
sector is concerned, there are five projects; Railways, there are 16; Roads 
and Highways, there is 1; Urban Development, there is 1; Petroleum, 
there are 2; Coal, there are 2; Health  and Family Welfare, there are 2; 
and, Fertilizers, there is 1. These 30 projects account for 95 per cent of 
the cost overrun.

*405. SHRI GHULAM NABI AZAD: Will the Minister of EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state:

terrorism; and 
(b) if so, the salient features thereof?

AFFAIRS (SHRI DIGVIJAY SINGH): (a) Yes.

Memorandum of Understanding was signed between the Government of 
the Republic of India and the Government of the Russian Federation on

for adoption.

has helped in processing large volumes of mails faster and in an efficient 
manner which in turn results in faster deliveries to addressees. 
To improve front office (counter) operations, the Department of Posts 
has already implemented a compre hensive technology induction 
programme with thrust area on computerization and on networking the 
bigger post offices, major sub-post offices, administrative offices and all

money order transmission has been introduced throughout the country.

introduced in large post offices. Induction of these machines has reduced 
long delays and made postal transactions more efficient and economical.

Traditional wireline solutions are increasingly supplemented by 
wireless technologies for providing connectivity in remote villages because 
of the number of advantages such as  maintainability etc. These include 
point to point Very High Frequency/Ultra High Frequency (VHF/UHF) Radio, 
Multi Access Rural Radio System (MARRS), Digital Enhanced Cordless 
Telecommunications (CorDECT), Code Division Multiple Access (CDMA) 
based WLL, INMARSAT, etc. 
Technology based on IEEE 802.11b/a/g standards hold promise for 
high bandwidth connection in the future. For this DIT has been carrying 
out a project called "Digital Gangetic Plains" implemented by IIT Kanpur 
to test out the viability of this techno logy for rural connection. The project 
aims to use the technology based on 802.11 b IEEE Standard working in 
the 2.4 GHz to 2.4835 GHz for providing wireless connectivity to villages 
in the corridor between Lucknow and Kanpur. Data up to a few Mbps 
throughput had been obtained through the wireless link and potential for 
setting up of rural information kiosks look promising, though economies 
are yet to be established.

Corporation of India has informed that the annual earning of the

allowance during the year  2002-03 is about Rs. 4 lakhs for a Handling

the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act (PFA) standards are distributed

Some complaints about the quality of foodgrains supplied under the 
PDS were received during the last three years. 
During 2000-2001, co mplaints were received from the State 
Governments of Arunachal Pradesh, Jammu & Kashmir, Karnataka, 
Sikkim and Tripura regarding supply of foodgrains of poor quality, especially 
rice procured under relaxed specifications (URS). Keeping in view the 
reluctance of consumers, the supply  of URS rice of 1997-98 Kharif 
Marketing Season was stopped. 
During 2001-2002, the Governments of Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, 
Maharashtra, Rajasthan and NCT of Delhi complained about the supply 
of "luster lost" wheat while the Government of Goa and Kerala complained 
about the poor quality of rice stocks. It was explained to the State 
Governments that, except in appearance, lustre lost wheat is as good as 
sound wheat, especially in terms of nutritional value. The FCI officers 
were instructed to ensure that rice of good quality only was supplied 
under the PDS to Goa and Kerala. 
During 2002-03, the Governments of Rajasthan, Delhi, Gujarat and 
Maharashtra had complained about issue of poor quality of "lustre lost" 
wheat under PDS and Government of Karnataka and Kerala had 
complained about the issue of poor quality of rice under various schemes. 
Keeping in view the reluctance of co nsumers, the issue of "luster lost" 
wheat for distribution under TPDS was stopped. FCI was instructed to 
ensure that rice of good quality only is supplied under the PDS in 
Karnataka and Kerala. 
(c) and (d) No, Sir. FCI stores foodgrains in scientifically constructed 
godowns under proper supervision of trained quality control officials who 
preserve the quality of foodgrains during storage. FCI has a standard 
procedure for issuing stocks under the "first in first out" principle. State 
Governments are free to inspect the stocks of foodgrains and satisfy 
themselves about their quality before lifting the same from FCI depots. 
The State Governments have also been advised to depute an officer not 
below the rank of Inspector to check the quality of stocks.

117 

RAJYA SABHA [21 August, 2003] 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI V. SREENIVASA 
PRASAD): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. In view  of the Report of Centre for Science 
and Environment (CSE), a Non-Governmental Organization, regarding 
presence of pesticide residues in the Bottled water, the Government had 
constituted an Inquir y Committee under the Chairpersonship of 
Smt. Satwant Reddy, Additional Secretar y in the Department of Consumer 
Affairs on 5th February, 2003. The Committee submitted its Report on 
25th March, 2003. The major findigns and recommendations of the Report 
in respect of functioning of Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) are as per 
Statement (See below,). The Government has accepted all the 
recommendations of the Inquiry Committee pertaining to BIS. 
Statement 
The major findings and recommendations of the 
Reddy Committee report 
* BIS has an established system for developing and formulating 
standards by involving different sector. Consensus is an essential 
procedural principle and a necessa ry condition for the preparation 
of Standards. Further BIS has adopted the International 
Organization for Standardization (ISO) Guide 7—1982 on the 
requirements suitable for product certification. The views 
expressed by the scientists, consumer organization and DGHS 
(PFA) on draft standards are taken into consideration. Overall, 
the prescribed procedure was fo llowed while formulating these 
two standards for Packaged Drinking Water. The BIS Secretariat 
has carried out its assigned function of identifying appropriate 
Sectional Committees, consulting the interested sectors, 
placement of comments before the Sectional Committee, and 
recording of the decisions re lated to each of the quality 
parameters. The standards have specified all those 
characteristics and requirements that are necessary, the required 
limiting values and also the test methods. 
* BIS certification for Packaged Drinking Water and Packaged 
Natural Mineral Water was made mandatory under PFA by Ministry 
of Health and Family Welfare through two Notifications issued on 
29th September, 2000. Before these Notifications were issued, 
118 

[21 August, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
the matter was discussed by experts in the Central Committee 
for Food Standards (CCFS), set up under Rule 3 of PFA Act. 
This Committee, under the Chairmanship of Director General of 
Health Services considered the BIS standards and found them 
adequate for adoption under PFA. The specifications for 
pesticides residue under PFA standards as well as BIS standards 
are "below detectable limit". 
* The Committee found that the standards for Packaged Drinking 
Water and Packaged Natural Mineral Water were adequate and 
the detection limits of pesticides  residue in these two standards 
compare favourably with pesticide residues in other food items 
such as milk, fruits, vegetabl es and foodgrain s, which account 
for a major portion of daily intake by human beings. For example 
existing test methods detect DDT in packaged water upto the 
level of 0.02 ppm, whereas in milk and milk products (on a fat 
basis), it is permitted upto 1.25 ppm under PFA. 
* The two standards on Packaged Drinking Water were formulated 
by deriving assistance from Codex and WHO guidelines. At that 
time Codex had not yet agreed upon the relevant test method for 
detection and determination of pesticide residues. Hence the 
concerned Technical Committee of BIS decided to adopt the test 
method standard established by another technical committee of 
BIS, which were prescribed for pesticides residues in fruits, 
vegetables and soils. These standard test methods were not 
specifically meant for drinking water. Since an agreed Codex 
test method was not available at that time, no individual officer 
or organization can be held responsible for this weak link in the 
test method adopted. 
* A pro-active approach towards keeping the standards dynamic 
and at par with international developments in related fields is 
necessary. This would ensure that BIS strives for continuous 
improvement of standards by providing for an in-built alert system, 
which would flag emerging problems before they assume 
threatening dimensions. 
* BIS should have a Core Group of Scientists from various fields 
with the responsibility of keeping track of recent scientific and 
119 

RAJYA SABHA [21 August, 2003] 
technical developments in critical areas. These scientists would 
alert the BIS management on the need to update and revise 
particular standards even before the review is due. 
* Draft standards should be put on the Website of BIS in order to 
obtain comments from all interested individuals and groups. This 
should be brought to public notice by giving advertisements in 
the print and electronic media. 
* The standard formulation is a voluntary activity and BIS does 
not pay anything, even in terms of TA/DA, for participation in 
meetings of the Technical Committees set up for standard 
formulation. As a result, at times, scientific organizations and 
consumer organizations are not able to participate in the meetings 
of Technical Committees. There is an  urgent need to take remedial 
measures to get over this problem. 
* The steps involved in the certification process as laid down in 
the BIS Act, Certification Regulations and Manual of Operations 
etc. have been followed in li censing the manufacturing units. 
Surveillance inspections and picking up of samples from the 
factory and the market place for assessing their conformity to 
the requirements of standard in a recognized laboratory have 
also been carried out. Instances of action taken, including 
stoppage of marking when non-compliance was observed, indicate 
that supervision and monitoring, required under the scheme were 
carried out. However, some shortfall was observed in the targets 
set for frequency of surveillance inspections and testing of 
samples. It has also been observed that in addition to the existing 
demands for certification, about 750 licences for Packaged 
Drinking Water were added for which additional resources like 
manpower were not provided. Constraints of manpower available 
for the over all certification and enforcement activities of BIS 
might, therefore, have contributed to the shortfall noiticed in the 
surveillance inspection. No single individual can be held 
responsible for this. 
* When BIS certification for an item of mass consumption like 
packaged water is made mandatory, it increases the responsibility 
and answerability of BIS towards the consumers. BIS should 
120 

[21 August, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
have a complete in-house review  of its resources before accepting 
this responsibility. Inadequacies of manpower and other resources 
should be identified and ways to fill up those gaps be explored 
before the challenge is accepted. But once BIS has accepted 
this responsibility, it must discharge it faithfully and not cite lack 
of manpower or resources as justification for non-adherence to 
the norms. 
* BIS prepares one Scheme of Testing and Inspection (STI) for 
each product, after due consideration of the specifications in the 
relevant standard but this STI, once prepared beco mes applicable 
to all licensees of that product. In the European directives, it is 
found that the frequency of sampling and analysis for water put 
into bottles or containers for sale varies according to the capacity 
of production. It is suggested that BIS may consider the 
desirability of linking the frequency of testing with the production. 
In other words instead of a single STI for all licensees, BIS may 
take into account the quality of raw water, the technology used 
for purifying and quantity of water produced in a day and develop 
a STI for that individual manufacturing unit. 
* BIS may consider setting up product specific committees, as 
prevailing in AFNOR (French Standard body), having provision 
for outside expert participation at least for certification of 
mandatory items. This will enable BIS to involve the mandating 
body, say PFA of DGHS or its nominee to advise on the STI, 
choice of testing laboratories and overall implementation 
effectiveness of the scheme. 
* In addition to BIS's Central Labo ratory, Sahibabad, services of 
13 other laboratories were made use of by BIS for testing of the 
samples drawn. It was necessary for evaluation of applications 
for grant of licence and for superv ision, the recognition of the - 
laboratories has been based on international standards regarding 
the competence of the testing laboratories. The laboratories have 
followed the testing methods specified in the standard and have 
submitted reports in the time in properly designed format 
indicating the specified value an d the values obtained for the 
samples submitted. 
121 

RAJYA SABHA [21 August, 2003] 
* The Bureau of Indian Standards, the National Standards Body of 
India, became functional as a statutory body under the Bureau 
of Indian Standards Act, 1986 with effect from 1 April, 1987 
taking over the staff, assets and liabilities of Indian Standards 
Institution established in 1947. For over 50 years this institution 
has been successfully promoting and nurturing the standardization 
movement in the country. It has provided for the harmonious 
development of standardization, marking and quality certification 
of goods. However, there is now a need for BIS to revitalize its 
core competencies. The existing procedures of BIS formulated 
several years ago are somewhat  shrouded in secrecy and 
confidentiality. Government is, however, committed to greater 
transparency. There is also a gr eater participation of people in 
decision making. The increased use of computers, the internet 
and websites has made it possible to reach out to people in a 
cost effective way. BIS should overhaul its procedures in the 
light of these developments and increase transparency in its 
operations. List of members of Technical Committees, draft 
standards, list of licensees and their present status may be put 
on its website and updated at monthly intervals. The possibility 
of placing test reports of samples drawn from factory or market 
on the web may also be considered. 
* In the developed countries, there is only one standard for drinking 
water and countries are expected to  ensure that all drinking water 
for human consumption, whether it is made available through 
the distribution network or in containers, conforms to those 
standards. It is time that the Government/Municipal machinery 
gears itself up to provide safe drinking water through its distribution 
network. 
* There is also need to review the permissible limits of contaminants 
in other food products under PFA. This may also lead to a wider 
discussion regarding permissible le vels of use of pesticides and 
fertilizers for agriculture and hortic ulture purposes. As long as 
pesticides and fertilizers are used for agriculture, they would 
have an adverse effect on food and water. 
* A water re-charging system shoul d be made mandatory for this 
industry. Some guidelines regarding selection of sites for 
122 

[21 August, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
installation of packaged drinking water industry are also required 
to ensure their location in pollution free areas. 
 When BIS establishes a standard, it must specify the 
corresponding test methods. In the amended standards 
(Amendment No. 4 of February 2003) it has been stated that 'the 
analysis shall be conducted by using internationally established 
test methods meeting the residue limits specified". This is vague 
and has left the choice of method to laboratories, which will lead 
to confusion, as it will not permit comparison between the results 
of different laboratories. BIS should constitute a committee of 
Experts from the leading research institutions like Central 
Pollution Control Board (CPCB), National Institute of Nutrition 
(NIN), Central Food 'Technology  Research Institute (CFTRI), 
Central Food Laboratories, Indian Toxicological Research Centre 
(ITRC), Indian Institute of Technology (NT), National 
Environmental Engineering Research Institute (NEERI) etc. 
engaged in evaluation of water quality for a review of the standards 
specified in IS: 13492 and IS: 14543 in order to specify the test 
methods to be followed by the testing laboratories.

Minimum wages for beedi workers 
†3117. SHRIMATI SAROJ DUBEY: Will the Minister of LABOUR be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that rates of the minimum wages in respect of 
beedi workers vary State to State; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; and 
(c) the steps Government are going to take to fix uniform rates of 
minimum wages in respect of beedi workers throughout the country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR (SHRI 
SANTOSH GANGWAR): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. There is variation in rates 
of minimum wages in respect of beed i workers from State to State, which 
is due to differences in socio-ec onomic and agro-climatic conditions, 
prices of essential commodities, paying capacity, productivity, local 
conditions influencing the wage rate etc. Beedi making is a scheduled 
employment in the state sphere. The variation in minimum wages is also 
attributed to the fact that the different State Governments are the 
appropriate Government to fix, revise and enforce minimum wages in 
scheduled employment including beedi making in their respective 
jurisdictions under the Minimum Wages Act, 1948. 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
169 

RAJYA SABHA [21 August, 2003] 
(c) In order to minimize the disparity in minimum wages in various 
regions of the country, the Central Government has issued guidelines for 
setting up Regional Minimum Wages Advisory Committees. In order to 
bring in uniformity in minimum wages, the Central Government mooted 
the concept of a national floor level minimum wage and fixed it at Rs. 35/- 
per day in1996 based on the recommendations of the National Commission 
on Rural Labour (1991) and subsequent rise in the price level. The national 
floor level wage is periodically revi sed based on the basis of increase in 
the Consumer Price Index. It was last revised to Rs. 50/- per day w.e.f. 
1.9.2002. The State/UTs have been requested from time to time to ensure 
that the minimum wage in none of the scheduled employments including 
beedi making is below the national floor level wage.

and social development through literacy, education, health, nutrition,

of the weaker sections of the societ y, etc., and (iii) direct attack on

  3138.  SHRI SUKHDEV SINGH LIBRA: 
           DR. ABRAR AHMED: 
Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to state : 
(a) the names of the States that have sought financial package from 
the Centre to meet the present financial crisis; and 
(b) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING (SHRI 
SATYABRATA MOOKHERJEE) : (a) and (b) During discussions at the 
Deputy Chairman-Chief Minister level for finalizing the Annual Plans of 
States, most of the States, in general, have sought enhanced Central 
Assistance for Plan financing to supplement the States Own Resources 
(SOR). However, the allocations of Central Assistance for the Annual 
Plans of States being based on Formul a/Criteria, State specific allocations 
are therefore, guided by the respec tive Formula/Criteria. Further, the 
schemes and projects of priority to  the States are also given due 
consideration while allocating Central Assistance for various Special and 
other Programmes of States. 
However, the Financial Mangement of the States being primarily the 
responsibility of the State Governments, it is for the respective States 
Governments to initiate remedial action. Nevertheless, in order to alleviate 
the mismatch in the States' cash flow , the Government of India releases 
plan assistance, share in Central taxe s and small savings loans in advance 
depending on the need and request of the State Government. In addition 
to Ways and Means support by Reserve Bank of India, Central 
Government also provide Ways and Means advances to States. 
Pursuant to the recommendatio ns of the Eleventh Finance 
Commission a Medium Term Fiscal Reform Plan (MTFRP) has been drawn 
up by the Government of India. Under the scheme, States have been 
encouraged to draw up a monitorabl e fiscal reforms programme aimed at 
improving their financial position in th e medium term. Incentive funds will 
be made available to States periodically depending on the progress in 
achieving fiscal reform targets.  Planning Commission has been 
impressing upon the States to observe fiscal prudence not only in the 
DCH-CM level discussions for finalizing the Annual Plans of the States 
but also during the official visits and periodic review meetings of the 
Commission with the States.

SHRIMATI SHABANA AZMI (Nominated): Madam, I rise in support 
of a uniform Civil Code based on gen der justice. Personal laws of all 
religions discriminate against women on matters of inheritance, divorce, 
maintenance, etc. Let us ca ll out just and equitable laws of all religions and 
have a blueprint that ensures just ice for all women. This should be 
discussed threadbare at the national level. However, this cannot be the 
Hindu Code imposed uniformly on all religions. Polygamy and Triple Talaq 
are unjust to women just as the advantage to the male members 6i the 
Hindu undivided family in property matters is unjust to women. Both will 
have to be dropped. It is argued that mi norities resist uniform Civil Code 
because they are reluctant to integrate with the mainstream. This is 
patently absurd. Does uniformity unde rmine or promote unity? The function 
of laws is to promote freedom and ens ure justice. National Integration can 
occur when minorities feel secure and have access to jobs, when their life 
and property is not jeopardised. Each time a communal riot is engineered 
when the guilty get punished and justic e is perceived to be done. However, 
women have waited for 56 long years for gender justice guaranteed under 
article 15 of the Constitution. Th is has eluded them because of 
discriminatory personal laws of all religions. If a uniform Civil Code can 
guarantee them this justice, let us  go ahead and demand a national debate 
with all stakeholders. In the absence of a blueprint no discussion can take

Madam, I rise to support this Constitution (Scheduled Tribes) Order 
(Amendment) Bill, 2003. I am very glad that the Bill will entitle the Bodos and 
the Bodo Kacharis of Assam, including the B.T.C. Areas District, and benefit 
them with the ST status. Madam, I will not confine myself to the issues of 
SCs and STs. After this amendment, some of .the tribes who are not 
included in the Scheduled Tribes list will be included. But my humble 
submission to the Central Government is, some other tribes who have 
migrated to the Bodoland territory from West Bengal, Orissa and Bihar 
should also be included in that list. I particularly know some tribes residing 
in Assam, which are not regarded as tribes. I mean to say, Madam, those 
who are tribals in Orissa, are regarded as non-tribals in Assam. The tribes 
of Assam are not there in West Beng al, but the tribes of West Bengal, 
Orissa and Bihar are residing in Assam. They are compelled to reside there. 
I know that the fore fathers of the hon. Chief Minister of Assam, Shri Prafulla 
Mahanta, were from the district to which I belong. But he was not a tribal. 
But those tribes, which are there in Assam, are not regarded as tribals. 
They had gone to Assam for their livelihood, to work in tea gardens, and in 
many ways, they were settled in Assam, but they are not regarded as 
tribals. 
Madam, my point is, suppose I am a tribal, under the Constitution, 
I enjoy the benefits of a tribe in Orissa, West Bengal and Bihar also. But if 
my uncle or my son goes to Assam, and if due to circumstances he resides 
in Assam, he will not be regarded a tri bal. This is the disparity which is seen 
in Assam, and also in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. As a member of 
the SC & ST Welfare Committee, I ra ised this point once again, when we 
were on a tour to Assam and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. It is not 
the question of it being a State subject. But when would a Constitutional 
Amendment be brought to this effect? A member of a Scheduled Tribe of. 
India is not from Bangladesh or Pakistan. He is a son of the soil. Under the 
Constitution, he enjoys the benefits of the tribe, but he is not regarded a 
tribe in Assam. 
Therefore,. Madam, my humble s ubmission is .that the Central 
Government should look into the matter. It must look into the case of tribals 
residing in Assam, especially the migrants, poor tribes, who were residing 
earlier in West Bengal, Bihar and Or issa, particularly, the Santhals, the 
Mundas, the Hose, the Kgals, the Bhumig, the Oraons and so many others. 
Madam, the sufferings they ate facing are beyond imagination. ऐसे आिदवासी

SHRI ANANDRAO VITHOBA ADSUL: Sir, this Bill has a very limited 
purpose, that is, amendment to Sect ions 21 and 22 of the NABARD Act, 
1981. The purpose of the amendment is to extend the agricultural credit, 
specifically, crop loan, up to Rs. 50,000 at the single digit, i.e., 9 per cent. 
As we all know in each and every sector, each and every bank is extending 
the loan facility at a lower rate of interest than used to be done earlier. The 
same demand was received from various corners of the country. We 
received   various   representations,    and,    accordingly,    the   Government'

[21 August, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
consulted the RBI and the NABARD, and, we came to the conclusion that 
for the agricultural credit, the loan facilities should be extended at the single 
digit rate. Accordingly, the commercial banks and public sector banks have 
accepted our proposal to extend this facility at the rate of nine per cent for 
crop loan of up to Rs. 50,000. As we  all know, a major portion of the 
agricultural loan is disbursed by c ooperative sector. Presently through 
NABARD, the refinance is made yearly  for about Rs. 6500 crores. But the 
procedure is that there are so many tier s, particularly, three tiers, in every 
State. The NABARD is extending loan s to the State Cooperative Banks, 
then the State Cooperatives extend to  the District Central Cooperative 
Banks, and then primary societies, and then the ultimate borrower comes. 
And, they are charging the transacti on cost. Initially, the NABARD is 
extending at the rate of 6-6.25 per cent, but it goes up to 14 to 16 per cent. 
And if we have to achieve whatever we have announced, then we have to 
reduce some tiers, and, that is why it is decided that the NABARD will 
directly extend this facility to Dis trict Central Cooperative Banks. And 
unless an amendment is made in the NABARD Act, 1981, it is not possible. 
And that is why, this Bill, was passed by the Lok Sabha, without any 
discussion. But fortunately, discussions have taken place in this House; I 
feel happy that so many Members have participated in the debate, 
particularly, Shri Parmar. Shri Ramachandraiah, Shri Kamaraj, Shri Viduthala 
Virumbi, Shri Ekanath Thakur, Shri Suresh Bhardwaj, Shri Verma. I honour 
the views expressed by the hon. Members here; they are valuable. And I 
accept the suggestions that have to be taken into consideration for the 
future. Yes, fortunately, the Governm ent is thinking about drafting a scheme 
for the rural cooperative sectors. 
Some of my hon. colleagues expre ssed the view that the limit that 
is up to 50 per cent, needs to be extended. Yes, it needs to be extended, 
but this is a beginning from the Government side. Secondly, it is a crop 
loan. The Government has announced other loans, which have no limit, but 
also stipulated that the rate of inte rest should not be above ten per cent. 
Not only that, the Government is thinking on the lines that if so many banks, 
the private sector and public sector ban ks, are offering loans for vehicles at 
low interest rates, then why should we not extend similar loans to farmers 
for tractors and other equipment and ma chinery too. With a group of other 
banks, State Bank is taking a lead for that purpose, and within a short 
period of time, our farmers will get these tractor loans, and loans for other 
equipment for agriculture at lower rates.
